definition: Moon Animator 2's 'Calculate Motion Paths' command (right-click context menu, with a choice of scope: the whole selected key range, or a window 'around' the current frame — the presenter's own stated preference, since the full-range mode 'gets a little hectic') draws a computed line directly in the 3D viewport tracing an effector's actual path over the chosen span, used here specifically to check and hand-fix a sword-tip's arc after a fast combo swing was posed.
purpose: Let an animator SEE the exact path an already-keyed effector traces through space, directly overlaid in the 3D scene, so an unintended kink, an overly-tight curve, or a good-but-not-quite-right arc can be spotted and hand-adjusted without guessing from the posed keys alone.
visible_effect: A drawn line (confirmed in this session's own frame at t=05:59 as a bright magenta/pink trace) appears in the viewport following the selected part's position across the chosen frame range, updating live as keys are adjusted.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Not applicable — an authoring aid, not a viewer-facing effect; the fixed-up arc it enables reads however a clean arc versus a broken one reads (see the existing `arcs` card).
physical_interpretation: A direct, exact visualization of the same path data a strobe photograph or onion-skin overlay approximates by other means — here the tool computes and draws it directly from the actual keyed transform data rather than from a human's visual estimate.
use_cases: checking and refining a fast action's arc (a weapon swing, a thrown object's path) immediately after a quick pose-to-pose block, before committing to the timing pass
any case where an animator wants to confirm an effector's path reads as a clean, intentional curve rather than trusting the posed keys alone to imply one
non_use_cases: checking a property that has no spatial path at all (an easing curve's timing shape, a texture swap) — this tool traces WORLD POSITION only
a rig or tool (like Cadence, see cadence_representation) where the same path data is already available as an exact reported number rather than requiring a drawn-and-eyeballed line
interactions: onion_skin_arc_verification (merged, W02) — the same underlying need (see an accumulated path to judge its shape) met by a different mechanism: that card's onion-skin is a 2D hand-drawn animator's technique relying on many overlaid drawings and a human eye; THIS tool computes and draws the path directly from exact keyed 3D transform data, no drawing or estimation involved — a strictly more direct, more exact version of the same verification instinct, one step closer to what Cadence's own measurement already does
single_frame_ghost_marker_for_spacing_reference (W08-71, this same batch) — a sibling Moon Animator visualization aid; that one shows a single frozen POSE, this one shows a continuous computed PATH
cadence_representation: Another case where Cadence's own existing measurement already IS the exact version of what this tool visualizes: `ai/motion.js`'s `bow_studs` (MOT-005) computes a path's exact perpendicular departure from its chord in studs, from the same kind of underlying transform data this tool traces as a line. The difference from the onion-skin case is narrower here: Moon Animator's motion-path line is itself already a COMPUTED overlay (not a human-estimated one), so the gap between it and Cadence's own number is purely about presentation (a drawn line an animator eyeballs vs. an exact reported figure) rather than about precision.
control_surface: `analyze_motion` reports `bow_studs` per part directly as a number; no tool in this build draws the equivalent path as a visual line in the viewport the way this reference tool does, which could matter for a human reviewer who finds a line easier to read at a glance than a number.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js` (`bow_studs`, MOT-005) already computes this measurement exactly; the video's own tool computes the same underlying path but presents it as a drawn line rather than a number.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — a read-only visualization; nothing in either Moon Animator's tool or Cadence's own measurement corrects a bad arc automatically.
failure_modes: trusting a fast, hastily pose-to-pose-blocked action's implied path without checking it, and only noticing an unintended kink once the motion-path line (or, in Cadence, the `bow_studs` figure) is actually checked — the presenter's own account is that this exact check-and-fix step was needed after the initial fast block ('right here what I'm going to do is I'm going to just fix up the motion path a little bit... make sure the arcs look fine')

using the full-range mode on a long or dense span and finding the result too visually cluttered to read ('sometimes it gets a little hectic') — the source's own stated reason for defaulting to the narrower 'around frame' scope instead
roblox_considerations: A Moon Animator 2 plugin-UI feature with no Roblox runtime equivalent — the drawn path is an editor-only visualization aid and is never present in the exported animation.
examples: the presenter right-clicks a set of keys and selects 'Calculate Motion Paths' after a fast, hastily-blocked sword-swing pose, naming the range-vs-around-frame scope choice directly and preferring the narrower one (video @ 03:20–03:34, confirmed in this session's own frame at t=05:59 showing a bright pink/magenta traced line in the viewport)
using the drawn path specifically to catch and hand-fix an arc that did not look right after the initial fast block (video @ 04:43–04:49)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/AH30avEEC9A @ 03:20–04:49 — Devgrams and Draco (the presenters) name and demonstrate the command directly, including both of its scope options and the specific reason for preferring one; the resulting path line is confirmed, if blurred by an in-video camera move, in this session's own frame at t=05:59; experimental until validated
